title: Anthropic mathematician posts Claude-assisted Riemann hypothesis proof; Stanford submits competing proof hours later
subtitle: Levent Alpöge's four-page note says a Claude-generated argument, formalized in Lean, closes the 1859 problem — and a Stanford postdoc filed an independent proof within hours.
author: AESOP AI Engine
body: Anthropic mathematician Levent Alpöge posted a four-page note on his personal website on November 20, 2026 stating that he and Claude had produced a proof of the Riemann hypothesis. The work began in early October and finished on November 16. The proof was formalized in Lean, the proof assistant that mechanically checks each step, and the Lean/Mathlib communities are reported to have accepted the formal artifact. A human-readable exposition has not yet been published, and independent peer review in the traditional journal sense is still in progress. Hours after Alpöge's announcement, Stanford mathematics professor Ravi Vakil said a postdoctoral researcher in his department had independently submitted a separate proof of the same hypothesis.

Why it matters is not that an AI 'solved math' — Claude did not act alone, and the proof must still survive expert scrutiny. The significance is the pattern. In August, Anthropic reported that an unreleased Claude model raised the proven lower bound on zeta-function zeros on the critical line from 41.6% to 67.2%, framing the work explicitly as 'not a proof of the Riemann hypothesis.' Three months later, Alpöge says the techniques closed the full result. That is the RH story in miniature: incremental improvements on partial bounds for 150 years, then a jump that may or may not hold up. The Lean formalization raises the floor on how skeptical the community can be while the natural-language write-up is being drafted.

The near-simultaneous Stanford submission is itself a datapoint. One of two readings fits: either the field was converging on the same ideas and both proofs reflect that, or at least one of them is wrong — and the wrong one tells us something about how conviction fails under AI-assisted collaboration. The last century of mathematics has seen several high-profile claimed proofs of RH that did not survive review; the base rate of 'announced then retracted' is not small. Expect both proofs to get picked apart line-by-line over the next weeks and months. The Millennium Prize's $1 million award requires publication in a reputable journal and two years of general acceptance, so even a correct proof takes time to officially 'land.'

A note for learners: the useful question is not 'did AI prove the Riemann hypothesis.' It is 'what does AI-assisted mathematics change about the pace and verification of major results?' Lean formalization gives a yes/no check that did not exist in Grigori Perelman's day. If Alpöge's proof is correct, the formal artifact is public and checkable by anyone with a laptop. The slow part is the human exposition — why the proof works, which ideas are reusable, what it unlocks. That is still a human job, and it will be where the real intellectual payoff lives for the next decade.
